The marimbaphone is a tuned percussion idiophone designed by the J. C. Deagan company of Chicago in the early twentieth century and now obsolete. It consists mainly of shallow steel or wooden bars in chromatic order, each with a tubular resonator underneath; the resonators for the wooden bars are shorter and the sound is close to the marimba, while the steel bars sound close to the celesta. It can be played with mallets, or the bars can be turned upright so that they can be bowed, the ends of the bars being concave; the same instrument can be played by several people at once in both ways. It was used mainly in marimba orchestras and for solo turns on the stage, and rarely in art music; Percy Grainger is one of the few composers who ever specified it.

In the early twentieth century the marimbaphone was developed by J. C. Deagan, Inc. of Chicago, Illinois, as a tuned percussion instrument that is now obsolete. Deagan also invented the steel marimba, a variant of the steel marimbaphone played only with mallets and not bowed. Both were displaced when the vibraphone appeared in 1921. It was little used in art music; Percy Grainger is one of the few composers who specified it, and the name is often miswritten in scores, usually meaning an ordinary marimba.
